summary:
FarmLine: NASA’s satellites, by text message.

Farmers must choose crop rotations years ahead while rain, heat and water supplies shift. The data that could guide them sits in archives they never open, and many farms have no internet. But every farmer can send a text.

FarmLine lets a farmer text one plain SMS from any phone, such as “alfalfa 89406, water is short”, and get back three three-year rotation options for their field: most water saved, most income, and safest in a drought. Behind the text, an engine combines 25 years of NASA POWER weather, USDA soil and cropland data, and real water allocations in a daily water balance. It tests every rotation against past droughts and projects it onto the field’s own climate trend to 2035. We checked its water use against OpenET satellite measurements, and it matched within a few percent.

FarmLine addresses Field Shift by turning NASA data into a decision a farmer can act on, in their own language, with no app, map or internet.
details:
What it does

A farmer texts their crop and ZIP code or town to a phone number. FarmLine replies by SMS with three

three-year crop rotation options for that field: the one that saves the most water, the one that earns the most, and

the one that is safest in a drought. The farmer can reply 1, 2 or 3 for details. It works on any phone with no

internet, and replies in English, Hindi, Urdu and Swahili, with other languages through checked translation.

How it works

1. Twilio delivers the SMS to a Cloudflare Worker, which checks the message is genuine and keeps a small

memory per farmer.

2. Google Gemini reads the free text and turns it into structured facts: crop, place, whether water is being cut, andwhat the farmer cares about most. Only the message text is sent, never the phone number.

3. A Python engine loads the field's data and runs a daily water balance (FAO-56 method) for every allowed

rotation: crop water need from NASA POWER weather, a soil-water bucket sized by the USDA soil survey, and

irrigation capped by the water allocation farmers actually received each year. That is 25 weather years times 11

sourced allocation years, 275 scenarios per rotation.

4. Water stress and soil salinity reduce yields; USDA yields and prices, university cost budgets and the irrigation

district's water charge turn them into dollars per acre.

5. The rotations are ranked (TOPSIS) by the farmer's priorities and the best three are returned.

6. Gemini words the reply from the engine's numbers only. A checker blocks any reply containing a number the

engine did not produce, and a fixed template is sent if the model is slow.

Checks built in

Hindcast: the engine plans as if it were 2020, then replays 2021 to 2023 with the weather and water cuts that

really happened, and compares its advice with staying in alfalfa.

2035 view: it measures the field's own temperature and rain trend over 2001 to 2025 (Mann-Kendall test, Sen's

slope), shifts the weather to 2035 and reruns the chosen options. At our demo field the trend is +0.3 C and +34

mm of rain per decade, and neither is statistically significant, which the plan states.

Validation: against OpenET satellite data for 2016 to 2025, our reference evapotranspiration is within +5.7% per

year (r = 0.992) and our alfalfa water use is within +1.6% on average in full-allocation years.

Benefits and intended impact

Farmers get a drought-tested decision instead of a dashboard. They see three options and choose for

themselves. Because the channel is SMS, it reaches farms with no internet and no smartphone. The intended

impact is less water used and more stable income when water allocations are cut.

Tools, languages and software

Languages: TypeScript, Python, SQL.

Twilio: SMS in and out.

Cloudflare Workers: receives the messages, checks they are genuine, runs the AI layer and sends the reply.

Cloudflare Durable Objects: one small memory per farmer.

Cloudflare AI Gateway and Workers AI: route the Gemini calls, with a Llama 3.1 backup model.

Google Gemini: reads the farmer's text, words the reply and translates. It never sets numbers.

Python engine (FastAPI, NumPy, pandas): water simulation, 275 scenarios per rotation, ranking, hindcast, 2035

view.

Vultr: hosts the Python engine (live), reached through a Cloudflare Tunnel.

Tiger Data (TimescaleDB): stores the field's weather, river flow and satellite series as hypertables with a monthly

continuous aggregate.

GitHub: shared code repository.

How it is creative

Most tools for this problem are web maps. FarmLine puts 25 years of NASA data behind the simplest interface

there is, a text message. The AI model is used only for language; every number comes from a tested engine and

is checked before it is sent.

Factors we considered

Access: no internet, any phone, the farmer's own language.

Honesty of the data: every number has a source, and years or values with no source are left out, not estimated.

Privacy: phone numbers are never sent to the AI model.

Limits: this is a prototype. Only one demo field is loaded (Fallon, Nevada, on the Newlands irrigation project). Thewater model is validated against satellite data, but the crop and cost tables still contain labelled regional proxies

and historical budgets, so the income figures are not validated farm advice yet. The engine is general; adding a

field means adding data, not code.
